Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. gentleman will agree that such a question might very well have had notice given in order to make it possible to give a very full report on the situation.
In so far as this conference is concerned, Canada will be represented at the meeting. The design of the conference was set forth in the state of the union speech of the President some weeks ago. I suggested the formation of a food bank to the end that by the establishment of such an institution surpluses would be stored against the probability of crop shortages or failures in the future. speechtext: I should like to direct to the Prime Minister a question of which I have sent him notice. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCE- MENT BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assume that the hon. member has reference to a press report that was issued by the co-chairmen of the international joint commission, namely Douglas McKay for the United States and Andrew McNaughton for Canada, in which were given the results of the commission's semiannual meeting which took place in Washington between April 7 and April 10. The only portion of the press release which deals with the matter in question is this:
Following its meeting with the Columbia board, the commission held further discussions concerning the formulation of principles for the determination of downstream benefits and their apportionment. The commission has now reached a mutually satisfactory basis for proceeding to a consideration of a first draft of principles. These principles will be discussed and further developed at the next meeting of the commission in Montreal on April 30.
The international joint commission, of course, is an independent international body which issues its own press releases. We have had no official communication by the commission with respect to the request made by the governments of the United States and Canada on January 29, 1959. However, I would point out to the hon. gentleman that the mutually satisfactory basis is not stated to be for an agreement between United States and Canada but for "proceeding to a consideration of a first draft of principles". In short, I assume that the commission is proceeding with the task assigned to it several months ago, and that in due course an official report will be made thereon to the two governments.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Regier.
(Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what are the outstanding facts arising out of the budget brought down last Thursday evening? In a speech which lasted almost two hours, and with his well-known aplomb, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) told us that, for the fiscal year ending March 31 last, his government had managed to come up with the largest peacetime deficit in our history. He confessed that his government had managed to reach an alltime record in regard to expenditures. He also pointed out that, by means of an entirely novel plan for the reconversion of part of the debt, his government had succeeded in raising to a more respectable level the interest rate on money. The minister of Finance also added that Canada's debt had increased considerably, that the Canadian standard of living is declining, that there are far too many unemployed, that the danger of inflation remains great, that production costs are too high, etc.
In fact no one could have done a better job of showing up the policy of bankruptcy which has been followed by the Conservative government since it took over in 1957. It was that policy of bankruptcy which prompted a Toronto paper to say last Saturday, with reference to the budget:
(Text):
No policy to guide it.
(Translation):
The newspaper went on to say that the Minister of Finance had been faced with a
difficult task. This we readily admit, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance did have to face a difficult task in preparing the estimates for 1959-60. His cabinet colleagues have spread money around rather casually, they have administered their departments in an easy-going way, they have promised favours right and left, with the result that the Minister of Finance had to ask the Canadian taxpayers to pay the piper.
The minister was therefore obliged to conclude his speech, on Thursday night, by saying that the deficit for the fiscal year 1959-60 would again be phenomenal, but that Canadians would get off, at least for the time being, by paying about $350 million a year in extra taxation. Nor did the minister fail to stress that of this increase of $2.3 billion in gross national revenue, he proposed to take in as his share no less than 23 per cent or to be more accurate an amount of $640 million.
The hon. minister took great pains to make it appear that the average Canadian would not be too much affected by this fiscal increase of $245 million for the current year and of $350 million for a full year. Now let us see how the matter stands. Here is what we note in table 8, page 2425 of Hansard. First, with regard to tax increases, in the field of budgetary levies, we note that personal income tax has increased by $54 million. We also note that corporation income tax has increased by $56 million. And we note further down the table that customs duties, sales tax and other duties and taxes, included in the budgetary levies, have increased by $46 million. And, in that field only, by a total of $156 million.
But, that is not all. As regards contributions to the old age security fund, we note that taxes have gone up by 50 per cent, since the personal income is being taxed by 1 percentage point with the result that instead of 2 per cent, each individual has to contribute 3 per cent to the old age security fund. And the corporation income tax has gone up also by 50 per cent. The same goes for the sales tax, with the result that in that field we note an annual increase of $196 million. And that table summarizes the increases in taxes as follows:
Personal income tax, $129 million; corporation income tax, $84 million; sales tax, $93 million; cigars, cigarettes and spirits, $46 million; and that, for an overall total of $352 million for a full year.



Now, who are those-and that is the interesting point-who will be called upon to pay this increase in taxation of $245 million for the current year or of $350 million for a complete year?
Mr. Speaker, here is the answer to that question: each and every one of the 4,600,000 Canadian taxpayers will be called upon to pay that increase in taxation. It will be the price of reality, as was so ably said by the honourable Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Canadians now realize that the Prime Minister could not carry out his promises, as the people believed he would. The people are now being asked to pay the price of reality.
That is why, the day following the budget speech, the man in the street, wishing to express his opinion on the recent events, made the following remarks: "That is too much", "It is an excess"; "We've had it", said another one; another one added that it was the last drop overflowing the cup and still another one said: "The party in power is the party of one man only". And the wisest of them all said: "I did not vote Conservative in the last election, because I knew what was coming".
Mr. Speaker, why has there been such a forthright reaction from the man in the street? This government's liberalities to the Canadian taxpayer, in the taxation field, for 1957-58, though they amounted to only a small fraction of what had been promised, have now been washed away and engulfed by the 1959-60 tax increase. As evidence of this, I am going to use the very illustrations used by the minister last Thursday night. As quoted on page 2417 of Hansard, the minister, having briefly mentioned the liberalities of 1957, quoted the following examples to illustrate the efforts I was mentioning a moment ago:
Taxpayers in the lower and middle income brackets will find that their tax increases this year will cost them less than the relief granted to them by the reductions of 1957.
And for purposes of illustration, the minister made this statement:
For purposes of comparison, let us consider the position of a typical married man who is the father of two children of family allowance age.
At an income level of $3,000 a year, under the new rates this man will pay a total of income tax and social security contribution of $56, an increase of $4 from the 1958 level. He will, however, be paying $34 less than he paid before the reduction we introduced in 1957.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I say that so far as income tax is concerned, that is the true
The Budget-Mr. Dumas situation, but the minister forgot to add that in the course of the year, the taxpayer will have to buy certain things, and will therefore have to pay the increased sales tax when the time comes to purchase a refrigerator, an electric range, or perhaps even a car or some other commodity. It can therefore be readily seen that not only will the taxpayer not pay less than before the 1957 deductions, but will now have to disburse more to pay for the tax increase.
Now if you take the case of the three other classes of taxpayers, those earning $4,000, $5,000 and $7,500, it must be concluded that the minister was not telling the whole story when he stated that the taxpayers would be paying less taxes, because there are some among them who will be buying a car, and they will have to pay for the increased sales tax.
In fact, it was no later than Friday, or immediately after the budget speech, that we were told the tax on cars would be raised by at least $25 to $30. So the poor Canadian, in the coming year, not only will be forced to return the few favours he enjoyed in 1957, but will have to reach into his other pocket and pay the difference through the amounts he will have to pay in the current year because taxes have been raised.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with regard to federal-provincial relations, the minister noted that since the house had discussed the matter at least twice during this session, he did not intend to again deal with the matter in his remarks. However, with apparent satisfaction, the minister put on record certain remarks that I am pleased to recall to him, and that are of particular interest to the taxpayers and people of the province of Quebec. We find at page 2410 of Hansard, that the minister said:
Under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act we are making unconditional payments to the provincial governments or unconditional tax abatements amounting to $684 million in the current year, of which $167 million is in the form of fiscal aid through equalization and stabilization payments.
It is to be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has said:
We are making unconditional payments-
Have you ever heard of anyone paying back a sum of money to some one he really owes it to and saying: "I'm paying this back to you unconditionally"? Who ever heard of such a thing? In fact, if the Liberal government had dared to use such a phrase in a

The Budget-Mr. Dumas budget speech, I do not know what would have happened, but I doubt that somebody would have raised his voice and talked about centralization.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the minister also seems to rejoice over the fact that the total conditional grants now reach $460 million, instead of the $136 million reached in 1956-57.
There again I presume that Quebec taxpayers are taking a wide-eyed look at this figure because they will never see a good part of those $460 million, at least not for quite some time.
In hospital insurance, the federal government will be making conditional payments of $160 million, of which the province of Quebec will not get a single penny.
In conditional payments for highways and transportation, the government will spend $70.3 million. We might get part of this for railway crossings, but the province of Quebec will get mighty little of this $70,300,000.
However, as regards item 7, in paragraph B, providing for conditional payment of $23.8 million for resource development, I do not believe that we shall see a single penny of that amount.
University grants will amount to $26.2 million, of which, of course, we will not receive a penny. Quebec taxpayers must indeed be vastly impressed!
And what will be the reaction of those who heard our hon. friends opposite say, when they used to sit on this side of the house: "What a bunch of centralizers", with reference to those who were managing the country at the time? But today, where are the true centralizers? I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Where are they? They are sitting there, on the other side of this floor.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to say a few words about our trade and about our foreign trade relations, especially with our neighbours to the south.
While in his budget speech the Minister of Finance dealt fairly at length with our international trade and our foreign economic relations, he practically said nothing about what action his government proposes to remove the uneasiness which is now being felt in our trade with the United States.
After saying that much of the increase in European gold reserves came from the United States and that this country was continuing

to act as a "good creditor", he said, and I quote from page 2408 of Hansard:
But it is to be hoped that the people and the government of the United States will become less timid regarding imports, particularly imports from a country like Canada, which buys from them far more than it sells, and is linked with them by bounds of common continental defence.
This is fine, Mr. Speaker, and the minister goes on:
In particular the actions of the United States in imposing during the past year new import restrictions on lead and zinc and mandatory controls on petroleum have aroused strong resentment in this country. We shall continue to press for the removal of these and other unjustifiable impediments to our export trade.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is rather a hesitant and lukewarm statement, and we wonder if that is all the government means to do.
In last year's budget speech, the minister was much more categorical. Let me quote a few paragraphs of his remarks at that time. I have before me the French Hansard for he 1958 session and I quote from page 1237 of volume II. The minister said this:
While access to the United States market has been improved in the last decade, and its tariffs have been significantly reduced entry into that market remains difficult and uncertain for many classes of goods produced in Canada.
Further on the minister added:
Perhaps most troublesome of all are the uncertainties arising from the many escape clauses in United States legislation and administrative practices. Hon. members do not need to be reminded of the recent restrictions imposed against Canadian oil and the continuing threat to our exports of lead, zinc and copper-notwithstanding firm trade agreement obligations.
When he said this, the minister was right. And a little further he stated:
We find it difficult to understand why the United States should treat its best customer and friendly neighbour in this way. We have made it clear to the United States authorities that measures which add to our difficulties in selling in the United States market or in third countries cannot but impair our ability and willingness to import from them.
That was, so to speak, a kind of threat. And the minister added:
This brief examination of the nature of our trading problems with the United States points up the need for vigorous action of a constructive nature. We intend to press for wider access on reasonable terms to the United States market; and we will continue to oppose with all the means at our disposal any threat to impose greater obstacles against Canadian exports to that market.
There again, Mr. Speaker, the minister was right.
At the same time we will continue to foster the growth and diversification of efficient Canadian

industries so that a constantly larger supply of our requirements may be met economically from domestic production.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what the hon. minister was saying last year; he gave the appearance of being quite firm. He appeared determined to convince his colleagues of the necessity of making certain representations to our friends to the south-at least that is the impression we got-and that he would lose no time about it. However, the excerpt I have just read from this year's budget speech, sings a rather different tune. The minister is now using the soft pedal. He does not say that the United States should buy more of our products, nor does he say that the government will continue insisting that the United States purchase more of our goods.
Mr. Speaker, we should realize-and this is most important, that many of the difficulties and problems confronting both the Canadian people and our friends in the United States are rooted in our trade exchanges.
In this regard let me give an example. I refer to the present unquestionable uneasiness in Canada about the future development of a particular industry, mining.
In that industry, and in the economy as a whole, inflationary pressures continue unabated and constitute a serious danger. Competition for the conquest of world markets is keener right now than it was before the second World War. Other ore-producing countries are developing their resources at a fast pace. However, in many of those countries wages and production costs are but a fraction of what they are in Canada.
Let us not forget for a minute that the mining industry in Canada is geared to export trade and that ore resources are valuable only to the extent that they are developed, put into production and marketed. Otherwise, they are but worthless rock.
The widest market for our mining products and for many others is unmistakably the United States. The contracts we are able to obtain in that field are awarded under terms imposed by the American administration as a result of pressures by the producers exerted by American producers who look upon those measures or restrictions as increased protection for their products, and even the very survival of their own industry.
Canadian mining companies hope for and anticipate the possibility of remaining the greatest suppliers of copper, zinc, lead, uranium and iron ore and many other metals in 66968-9-170
The Budget-Mr. Dumas the United States, for many generations to come, on an ever increasing basis.
However, Mr. Speaker, Canadian producers are worried, and I would even say greatly worried. They naturally realize the difficulties we have to face at this time and which are caused by that protectionist policy of our neighbours to the south. But their concern goes further than this. Canadian producers are wondering whether the Canadian government is actually taking the necessary steps to avoid a still more detrimental policy on the part of the American administration.
We might get an answer to this question when we know the attitude the U.S. government proposes to take with regard to the options which the United States atomic energy commission is holding in respect of Canadian uranium production after 1962 and 1963.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian uranium industry is admittedly facing great difficulties, especially as regards the period following the years 1962 and 1963, when the sales contracts with the Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited will have expired and, hence, as regards arrangements between this corporation and the United States atomic energy commission.
The Canadian uranium industry has developed amazingly in the last three years. It now ranks first among metal and ore producers in Canada in dollar value of exports.
During 1958, the value of uranium exports was no less than 5 per cent of all Canadian commodity exports.
The following figures show how much that industry has advanced. In 1957, uranium exports reached a total of $131 million, as compared to $260 million in 1958. For the current year, and taking into consideration the number of mines and plants holding production contracts, our uranium exports will probably reach the $350 million mark.
We know that uranium producers have contracts with the Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited to the value of $1,500 million, and that the latter, in turn, has contracts for a similar value with the United States atomic energy commission. Therefore, it is evident that the United States is our main purchaser of Canadian uranium.
General opinion seems to indicate that in the next ten years the uranium market, for civilian purposes, will be fairly insignificant compared to the productive potential of mines.

The Budget-Mr. Dumas
So, for a period of six to eight years, that is from 1962 and 1963, after the contracts with the Eldorado Mining have expired, there will be a gap.
In addition to its existing contracts with the Eldorado Mining the United States atomic energy commission has options on a large portion of the uranium potential of Canadian mines for the period subsequent to the lapsing of its contracts, that is until December 31, 1966.
The commission will thus be in a position to take advantage of those options until March 31, 1961.
We all know that if that industry has reached its present development, it is because of the demands and representations of the United States government which wanted to provide for its own basic requirements of uranium oxide. Canadian uranium companies have therefore every reason to impress upon the Canadian government the necessity for the United States government to take up its options on Canadian production until December 1966, and to do so with the least possible delay.
That is most important, Mr. Speaker, and in this connection, I should like to refer to a brief submitted to the Canadian government about two or three months ago. In that brief the Canadian Metal and Mining Association outlined as follows the Canadian producers' approach to this matter:
(Text):
As the civilian market for uranium up to 1966 will be very limited, it is of vital importance to the Canadian uranium industry that these options be taken up. It is respectfully requested that the Canadian government examine this situation and bring to the attention of the United States government the importance its attaches to the taking up of the options before March 31, 1961, and the desirability of giving notification of its intention to do so at the earliest possible date.

It is dated January 1959. This shows how important it is that the government make representations at the earliest possible moment.
I should like to say a few more words about our Canadian uranium industry. I would have liked to deal with the subject more extensively, but I notice that my time is fast running out.
Did the government take action on that recommendation of the Canadian Metal and Mining Association?
Is the Canadian government doing something to induce the United States government

to amend its apparently ever-expanding protectionist policy? Or will Canada's own trade policy turn to protectionism? That is the question raised by the budgets brought down in this house by the Conservative government since it gained power in 1957.
This afternoon, in reply to an inquiry from the Leader of the Opposition, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) stated-much to my surprise-that only on one occasion had he met with officials of the atomic energy commission in the United States. And yet, everyone knows how important it is to urge the U. S. government to let us know whether it intends to take up its options on Canadian uranium production after 1962 and 1963. This is of the greatest importance. If we fail to get a statement from the U. S. government as to its intention of instructing the A.E.C. to take up its option, there is grave danger that several mines located in the constituency of the Leader of the Opposition will be forced to close down, and then, only the mines with very high grade ore will be in a position to continue production.
In the light of recent developments, Canada is more than ever in need of assurances so that large segments of the Canadian economy might not be adversely or seriously affected as result of certain decisions that might be taken in the United States. In the case of Canadian uranium purchases by the United States, American producers are exerting pressure to prevent the options I have mentioned from being taken up. And to think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has only just met with officials of the United States atomic energy commission! That is astonishing! Moreover, we expect and demand that the Canadian government take all necessary steps to insure that these options be taken up as soon as possible.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, we must resist any pressure tending to curtail future trade between Canada and the United States.
Besides, to the extent allowed under existing legislation and essential administrative principles of both countries, it is important that consideration be given to the possibility of easing certain restrictions which have already caused some misunderstanding and which are apt to give rise to more.

same. We were both in a business recession causing acute unemployment, with the added complication in Canada of more rigorous climatic conditions severely restricting construction in the winter months. Yet despite this major handicap, because of government action our record is one of which we may well be proud.
This parliament has voted a further $250 million to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for housing purposes, bringing the total made available to date to an even billion dollars. Without in any way reducing the tempo of home building, I should like to see more emphasis placed on providing housing for old age pensioners and those in lower income brackets. In my opinion C.M.H.C. has not adequately promoted or publicized the use of the limited dividend section of the National Housing Act, whereby the government will loan up to 90 per cent of the cost of low rental housing. Limited dividend projects are usually sponsored by non-profit organizations such as churches, legion branches, service clubs and other public spirited bodies, but to date the number of such projects has been far too few in relation to the need. It is true that in 1958 more money was spent in this field than in any previous year but this amount, some $49 million, falls far short of satisfying the demand for this type of accommodation.
Limited dividend housing is relatively low-cost rental housing, but it is not subsidized housing. Subsidized housing is a joint municipal-provincial-federal project with the three governments sharing in the capital cost and in the subsidy required to cover any operating losses. In addition there is provision for the federal government to contribute 50 per cent of the cost to a municipality in acquiring and clearing slum areas for redevelopment programs.
It is in these three areas of slum clearance, subsidized rental housing and low-cost but non-subsidized rental housing that more activity is required because the need is so great. Present restrictive regulations, such as the one limiting old age pensioners to 20 per cent of the total accommodation of a subsidized housing project to prevent so-called "islands" of elderly citizens, prevent full utilization of provincial help designed to provide housing for senior citizens only. The financing of limited dividend projects by non-profit organizations should be made easier by allowing prospective tenants to

subscribe part of the initial capital if they wish and are able so to do. Above all, an intensive promotion program by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is required to acquaint services clubs, legion branches, churches and other possible sponsors as to how they can help to provide decent housing accommodation for families in need, at a price they can afford.
A peculiar feature of our Canadian economy is the effect our long and severe winter has on employment, particularly in the construction industry. Therefore we have each year our peak unemployment in winter months. This government has tried to combat this by extending unemployment seasonal benefits to make them payable from the first week in December to May 15, in place of from the first week in January to April 15 as was the case under the former government. It has often been said that the former Liberal government were out of touch with the Canadian people. I would suggest they were also out of touch with the reality and severity of the Canadian winter.
A second attack on the problem of winter unemployment was the joint municipal-federal winter work program. Under this program the government agreed to pay half the labour costs of approved municipal projects carried out in the winter months. Let me make it clear that this refers to paying half the cost of additional jobs; that is, for labour specifically hired for the approved project, labour which would not have had a job if the project had not been started. As of March 20, 1959, as we were informed by the Minister of Labour, a total of 32,000 jobs have been provided under this scheme, and of the total of 1,909 applications from municipalities across Canada, 1,838 applications or 96 per cent were approved.
The scheme was deliberately designed to give the greatest federal help to those projects which would have the highest new labour content and so help the most in combating seasonal unemployment. Parliament voted $15 million to cover the cost of the program, and it appears that the greater part of these funds will be expended when the program ends on May 31. I hope the program will be reinstated next winter, when the experience gained in this first year of operation will allow an even more successful program. Planning should be started as early as possible so that a well thought out program will be ready for implementation as soon as the proper time arrives.
The Budget-Mr. Broome
Mr. Speaker, from Canada's earliest history Canadian expansion has been geared to high levels of foreign trade and to massive capital inflows required to finance and stimulate the growth in our economy. Because the greatest part of our capital inflow now comes from the United States, and because the greatest part of our trade is with the United States, the Canadian economy is highly sensitive to United States business cycles. The current recession which had its birth in the United States was well under way when this government first took office. The financial critic for the Liberals, in commenting on the budget statement of the Minister of Finance, had this to say at page 2456 of Hansard:
He did not tell us that carloadings in the United States, compared with last year, are up almost six per cent but in this country our carloadings are down. The Financial Post of March 28 pointed out that the United States industrial production will likely get back to its boom-time peak within a matter of days but by contrast Canadian output is only one-half up to its low in recovery.
I suspect what is meant is only one-half up from its low in recovery.
Let us examine this statement to see what did happen. The complete story is that industrial production started to drop in Canada early in 1957 but did not start to drop in the United States until after August of that year. This drop in production in Canada was therefore well under way by the time the first Conservative administration was formed. Through government measures outlined by the Minister of Finance consumer expenditure, which is much the largest and most stable element of demand in our economy, was maintained at a high rate and the drop in industrial production was halted at a point 6.6 per cent below the previous record level. In contrast in the United States, though the drop in industrial production started eight months later than in Canada it fell twice as far, namely to 13.1 per cent below the previous record. The Financial Post article which the Liberal critic quotes states that United States production has regained all but 1.5 per cent of its decline. This may be true; indeed I hope it is. In regard to Canadian industrial production, however, according to dominion bureau of statistics figures the industrial production index as of January, 1959 was 157.2 as compared with the previous peak of 159.6, showing that we also are about 1.5 per cent below our all-time record.
In regard to carloadings, it is true we are down from last year. According to dominion bureau of statistics figures carloadings' for

The Budget-Mr. Broome the first three months of this year were 828,516, as compared with 829,079 last year. We are therefore down one-twentieth of one per cent. I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker that the ground for this criticism was not well chosen. If the Liberals wish to compare the effects of the recession in the United States and Canada I suggest they read the Bank of Montreal Business Review of February 24, 1959, or Labour Research of August, 1958, a bulletin published by the Canadian Labour Congress. Both these issues are devoted to a comparison of the recession in Canada and the United States. In almost every comparison both publications show that the recession in Canada was less severe than in the United States.
We are not trying to minimize the effect of the recession in Canada, with the resulting slow-down in business and employment and the hardships Canadians are suffering as a result. We do say that what a government can do to help, that we have done. We have been aided in this by helpful suggestions from labour, management, interested organizations and ordinary citizens. In fact we have received constructive ideas from almost every group except the opposition, who have given us a great deal of destructive criticism.
I have already indicated the close dependence of our economy on the United States and our sensitivity to business fluctuations in that country. We are the fourth largest trading nation of the world and are more dependent on export trade than any other nation, in that one out of every five Canadians is directly dependent on export trade to keep his job. The United States is our biggest customer and supplier, selling us 70 per cent of our imports and buying 60 per cent of our exports. Although our imports from the United States were down 11 per cent in 1958 compared with 1957, we still bought more from the United States last year than we did in the boom year of 1955. In fact we bought $660 million more from the United States than the United States bought from us.
In 1957, despite our position as one of the leading manufacturing nations of the world, we imported fully finished manufactured goods to the tune of $262 for every man, woman and child in the country. By comparison the British figure was $48 and the United States figure a mere $28. It is my conviction that the overwhelming ownership of Canadian manufacturing facilities by United States firms tends to restrict the natural expansion of these subsidiaries in serving both domestic and export markets. The


tendency is for the parent company to continue to supply fully manufactured products to its subsidiary long after the Canadian market has grown to a point where local manufacture is possible and profitable.
There are other problems in regard to United States-Canada relations, such as the United States wheat disposal program, restrictions on imports of Canadian oil and base metals, the imbalance in trade between our two countries, and of course the question of continental defence. We have been accused by the opposition on the one hand of having an ultra-nationalistic point of view and thus antagonizing the United States, and on the other hand we have been accused by the opposition of having a very subservient attitude in regard to defence problems.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that they cannot have it both ways. Our policy of bringing our problems with the United States into the open for frank discussion has resulted in a better understanding by the United States of Canadian economic conditions. We have stood up for Canadian rights and in so doing we have earned the respect of the American people. We are no longer taken for granted. At the same time we have been realistic enough to acknowledge that in matters of continental defence we must play a lesser role and merge our defence system with that of the United States. This is only common sense and it is in the interest of the preservation of both our countries and our common way of life. In both these attitudes, I submit, we are serving the best interests of Canada. We shall continue to press for more independence in the operation of foreign subsidiaries in Canada to the end that these subsidiaries shall be operated in the best interests of Canada and that they shall be, as far as possible, truly Canadian operations.
Much has been said about our overwhelming dependence on the United States market. We have frequently been told that we place all our trading eggs in one basket and that it would be the mark of common prudence to try and diversify our trade pattern. To this end the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) took the leadership in calling a commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal last September, the first such full scale commonwealth conference on trade and economic problems to be held since 1932. It was the largest commonwealth conference ever held and indeed one of the largest international conferences ever held in Canada.
The sterling bloc represents the greatest single trading area in the world today. Close to half the world's trade is conducted in sterling, but up to now we have had extreme

difficulty in penetrating this market primarily due to quotas and currency convertibility restrictions.
As a result of this conference there was an immediate freeing of trade channels between Canada and the United Kingdom, culminating in the decision of the United Kingdom government in December to make sterling convertible. An immediate result of the conference was the sale of the record British Columbia salmon pack to the United Kingdom. Another result is commented upon in a Financial Post article in the April 11, 1959 issue, stating that Australia has relaxed quota restrictions against Canadian goods for the third time since last fall when the conference was held. We had an expanding trade with Australia up to the second world war. The war broke this trade pattern and it was not restored because of Australian import restrictions. The Liberals in their preoccupation with trade with the United States, neglected commonwealth trade. We propose to build up this trade and I believe a good start has been made.
There is one thing certain and that is if we wish to sell we must be prepared to buy. In this regard it is interesting to note two recent announcements. The first was by International Harvester and said that in future heavy duty trucks would be manufactured in Hamilton, rather than imported from the United States. Also, in place of bringing in United States diesels to power these trucks they would use Rolls Royce engines imported from the United Kingdom. The second announcement was by Cummins Diesel, one of the largest diesel manufacturing companies in the world, which stated their Canadian organization would, in future, purchase diesels from the Cummins subsidiary in the United Kingdom rather than from the parent plant in the United States. It appears that private United States industry recognizes our need to diversify our trade pattern, to correct in part our imbalance of trade with the United States, even if the official opposition does not.
Mr. Speaker, high levels of employment are neither reached or maintained in automatic fashion. Inflation must be held in check if our standard of living is to be protected. The government must continue to be vigilant in holding down governmental costs and industry and labour, while each guarding its own special interests must work together in the overall interests of Canada. If this is done, we will be able to maintain high levels of employment in an expanding economy and with a constantly rising standard of living.

Mr. Speaker, on March 26, I received my copy of the local newspaper, the Timmins Press, and
The Budget-Mr. M. Martin I received a very rude shock when I glanced at the headline featured on the front page which read as follows:
Pensions May Cause Tax Boost
The first paragraph of that article stated:
Canadians may be in for a round of higher federal taxes aimed at making the old age pension fund pay its way-
That part of it is very true but the fact remains that there appears to be a deliberate attempt on the part of this newspaper which has always been extremely friendly toward the present government to create the impression that present tax increases announced in the budget presented to the house last week were caused by the poor old age pensioners. What a change from the impression which was given to us and to the old age pensioners by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the past.
We well recall when the last increase of $9 in old age pensions was authorized. The impression given to the house and to the Canadian people was that this was merely an interim measure to tide us over until the government could tidy up the affairs of the country and then the old age pensioners could really look forward to something much better. As the months went by nothing was done and the question was handed over to a royal commission. Finally, after many long months of waiting, the report of that commission was handed down. That was some time ago but to date we have not heard a word about what this government is going to do for the old age pensioner although, as I say, scare headlines now appear in Conservative newspapers across the country which seek to blame the old age pensioner for present tax increases. The old age pensioner has received no increase in his pension but has been the recipient of blame for present tax increases.
I ran across another very interesting item this morning in what is probably the leading Conservative newspaper of the host of such newspapers across the country. The article appeared on the editorial page and the first paragraph stated:
In the wake of last week's dominion budget, leading companies in two major industries-oil and rubber-have increased the price of gasoline and tires. Tax increases were the decisive factor in each case.
I refer, of course, to the Globe and Mail, issue of today's date. Here we have a deliberate, bald-faced statement by companies in two of our leading industries that they

The Budget-Mr. M. Martin simply will not be taxed because immediately upon the announcement of increased taxation they announced their intention of passing the tax on to the consumer. I do not have figures concerning the amount by which they increased their prices so I have been unable to compare the increase in price with the increase in tax. I do not know if the price was raised sufficiently to equal the tax, or if it was raised three times as much as we have seen in many cases in the past.
A favourite preoccupation of newspapers of this political flavour, and particularly the Globe and Mail, over the years has been to blame labour for everything. I wonder what would have happened if the Canadian Labour Congress had immediately announced, as these companies did, that it refused to accept the increased taxation and that the increase would be passed on to the consumer through the medium of the congress immediately seeking raises in pay across the country? Would the Globe and Mail have written an editorial in defence of its action as it did in the case of these companies to which I referred?
Certainly the working people have as much right to pass along increases in taxes as has any company. The editorial goes on to point out how justified these companies are in taking this action. Incidentally, the editorial also points out how foolish hon. members of this group are in attempting to tax corporations. The editorial states very clearly that as soon as corporations are taxed they pass the increase on to the consumer and therefore they ask what is the sense of taxing them. The suggestion is that one might as well tax the consumer in the first place and be done with it.
One thing this editorial has accomplished has been to explode the carefully prepared and promoted theory that obtained across Canada that this was the small man's or working man's budget that laid off the little man and went after the big fellow. Within a week of the bringing down of the budget the Globe and Mail, the leading Conservative newspaper in Canada, has come out with an editorial stating that this was not the case at all because even before the budget debate concluded in the house many companies have already taken action to pass the increases on to the consumer, the little man for whom the government was supposed to have shown consideration in this budget.
These tax increases and especially those that are passed on by the corporations to the Canadian consumer lead to nothing other than a further boost in the cost of living, a general rise in prices and an increase in the so-called danger of inflation that threatens us. The greatest criticism one could offer this government, a criticism it has justly deserved,


is that it is seeking to avoid facing up to the two most vital problems in the country. It presents them in a rosy hue and attempts to make believe they do not exist. I refer, of course, to the problems of inflation and unemployment which are closely interwoven. The combination of these two elements gives rise to an even greater danger to our way of life and that is the growing economic offensive of the Soviet union. A British economist of note, Barbara Ward, broadcasting on the C.B.C. T.V. on April 5, 1959, had this to say:
If the west could achieve stability along with economic growth we would have little to fear in the threat from soviet economic offensive. Indeed such an offensive would be a good thing not only for the world but for the west as well.
It is very obvious that we have not achieved any stability in the past and certainly the government is not taking any serious steps to try to achieve any stability in the future. With this lack of stability we see the hard fought gains in welfare and security measures falling by spurts over very short periods of time, with the whole situation leading to more and more unemployment.
This so-called inflation we have at the present time is a new phenomenon. It is no longer the old-fashioned inflation of too much money chasing too few goods. What we have in its place now is a case of sellers overcharging for their surplus products. There is only one reason for it and only one reason can exist in this country today. The reason is that today in this country we have price control by big business, with organized labour fighting for its life to maintain its position and by so doing giving big business an alibi to maintain its prices. The trade union movement in this country is tied to business just as the tail is tied to the dog.
The Prime Minister was supposed to have recognized this new situation when he spoke at the Canadian Labour Congress convention in the city of Winnipeg just about a year ago. At that time he made an appeal to labour and business to hold the line, and he was supposed to have recognized the new situation which is arising. If we find that our inflation is the old-fashioned type, then the Prime Minister's appeal last year would have no meaning whatsoever because the natural process of supply and demand would straighten out matters and would bring things back into equilibrium. But the Prime Minister made his appeal to labour and to business. The chief difficulty was there were no businessmen present; there were only labour representatives. That is why there has been no record of the Prime Minister giving the same speech to the Canadian Manufacturers Association. It is very similar, Mr. Speaker, to a referee stopping a fight by throwing one man into the penalty box and letting the other man go

free. It was recognized as such. Certainly business did not curtail itself in any way and as a result labour followed suit. We have just carried on in our own regular, merry way.
The most important thing is that prices are not rising because of the pressure of buyers. Prices are rising today because of the pressure of sellers. We have a sellers' inflation instead of a buyers' inflation. What we see is that each and every day sellers are engaging more and more in strenuous and furious activities and we find that business people are able to do everything except lower their prices. This situation was recognized by our Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his remarks the other day, as reported at page 2408 of Hansard, when he said:
Advancing technology might have been expected to reduce the cost and selling price of many products to consumers. It is evident, however, that developments in corporation pricing policies, in labour organization and even in our political democracy are producing increased rigidities which inhibit the free play of competitive forces and thereby promote inflation and price increases.
I think the minister put his finger very close to the sore spot here, but we notice again that labour is brought in and given almost equal billing with business when actually, as I said before, the only thing that labour is trying to do is to hang on by the coat tails in this society of ours today. Labour is part of the cycle but labour is no more responsible for it than the tail is responsible for the mad dog which exists in our society today.
In the face of this phenomenon which we see rising, it is no wonder that the Liberal cure as applied to this situation was of no effect. I refer to the cure of high interest which the Tories like to refer to as the tight money policy. It did not work and it could not work because it was an old remedy for a new disease. It was trying to use a cold cure to cure pneumonia. The Canadian people realized that this scheme would not work and they got themselves a new physician, and they are now under the tender care of the Minister of Finance. When we look at it very closely we find that we still have a cold, we still have pneumonia, we have bronchitis along with it and the odd bit of flu. The result of all this treatment by the minister has not been a reduction in prices; it has not contributed to the general employment; in fact, it has retarded our economic growth.
In spite of all the fine words of the Minister of Finance, employment and inflation, or the high cost of living, whichever you prefer, still remain two of our biggest problems. Before any improvement can be hoped for
The Budget-Mr. M. Martin the government has first to recognize the problem which so far they have not done and, second, they have to do something about it. So far, I am sorry to say, the government obviously proposes to do neither.
The minister is very industrious. It took a very industrious man to dig out all of the statistics necessary to paint such a rosy picture as he painted the other night. Unfortunately, it has an ominous ring. This prosperity around the corner is something we heard about all during the 1930's. I hope we shall not have to listen to it again during the next 10 years.
There is another very important problem, Mr. Speaker, which apparently has been given no consideration whatsoever, namely the problem of education in this country. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton), and the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) during the throne speech debate outlined very clearly what we are facing with regard to our educational standards across the country as compared with those behind the iron curtain. This problem is confined, not only to secondary schools, which this special report dealt with, it applies also to our universities across the country which are finding it more and more difficult to make ends meet. If we go back to Hansard for March 4, 1959 we find that I asked the Minister of Finance the following question, as recorded at page 1596:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance which arises out of an article on page 1 of the Vancouver Sun of February 24, 1959. The question is this. In view of reports that the University of British Columbia finds it necessary to increase its fees by $100 per student next year, and in view of the prospect that other universities may find it necessary to do likewise, has the government considered the necessity of increasing its grants to universities in order to ensure that Canadian youth have every opportunity to obtain an education commensurate with their ability?
Now, the minister's answer at that time was as follows:
Without taking the time to comment on some of the questionable assertions contained in this question, I can only say that no consideration has been given to the subject.
Apparently, Mr. Speaker, we are still in the same situation. There has been no consideration given to this subject. I do not know to what the minister was referring when he spoke of the questionable assertions in my question, but I have done a little checking since that time and I find that since this government took office the following universities have had to raise their fees: The University of British Columbia, McMaster University, Toronto University, Assumption University, Windsor, University of New Brunswick, Carleton and Ottawa universities. The increase in fees ranges from a low of $25 at Ottawa University, to a high of

The Budget-Mr. M. Martin $100 at the University of British Columbia or possibly the increase at McMaster and Toronto which was 10 per cent.
X think it is obvious to all hon. members that we are moving more swiftly all the time toward a technological age. The days, relatively speaking, of the pick and shovel are over. The wealth of tomorrow is going to be produced by brainpower rather than by manpower. I noticed that today the Prime Minister, in answer to a question from one hon. member, gave a similar answer to that which the Minister of Finance gave last month, that is that no consideration has been given to this problem. I would like to know why. There is no question but that the government knows about this problem. It has been pointed out very clearly by members from their own side. It certainly has been pointed out time after time by members of the opposition. It has been pointed out in newspapers across this country from coast to coast. When is this government going to realize that there is a problem in this field, or are they going to sit back and let the iron curtain countries outstrip us completely in this field?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that this is government policy to ignore the problems, to paint rosy pictures and, possibly worst of all, to embark upon a deliberate policy of raising interest rates across this country. As we have seen, the government has no money for old age pensioners. They have no money for the civil servants. They have no money for the western farmers. They have no money, relatively speaking, to spend on unemployment. They have no money for education. They have no money for health insurance. I hear an -hon. member mention small business. There is another one that I left out. What is more, he is right; they have no money for these purposes. But it is no wonder they have no money, because all their money has gone to the money lenders of this country. There is nothing left for the essential services or to meet the serious problems of this country.
We had the example of the bond conversion last year. The terrifying costs of this conversion were outlined very well by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson). This subject was raised first, you may recall, by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) last year, and then by me, when we spoke in the budget debate. I well recall the contribution made to that debate by the Minister of Finance. All he could do was say "rubbish" and "poppycock".
What has been done as a result of this policy? Let us first of all take a look at

the treasury bills. I have here a weekly listing, starting with the week of January 7, 1959 and going up to the week of April 8, 1959. We see that treasury bills in Canada have risen in that time from 3.25 up to 4.42 as of April 8. Many questions were asked of the Minister of Finance during the last couple of years, and particularly in the last two months, concerning this problem. We heard various answers to the effect that this rate fluctuates from week to week; that it is dependent on the United States, and so forth. We have in this list a comparison of the spread on treasury bills between Canada and the United States over that same period of time. This spread has widened from 57 cents on January 7 to $1.47 on April 8. I should like, Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house, to include this table in Hansard for today.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in examining the budget, it would appear to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has done a very fine job in his method of taxation for the current year. He has made reductions where possible and has increased taxation where necessary. If one looks over the places in which he has increased taxes, one finds that he has increased from two per cent to three per cent the taxes on incomes, corporations and sales to meet the needs of the huge deficit in our old age security fund. Surely, there is no one in this house who will raise any objection to making this portion of our social security program self-supporting.
Then the minister has increased the excise tax on cigarettes by two cents per package of 20. I am not sure that this increase should not have been greater because it would serve as an added deterrent. I think this is a wise move in view of the great volume of medical evidence that has accumulated on cigarettes and the harm which is suspected as a result of smoking them. Surely no one will disagree with the increase of 12 cents per quart bottle of whisky. Personally, I would feel that this increase could have been doubled because 90 per cent of the liquor drinking is social or compulsive and less than 10 per cent has any medical basis. In many cases the use of alcohol results in a long line of social
The Budget-Mr. Rynard
expenditures by governments for the treatment of alcoholics. In many cases broken homes are the result, diseased bodies, loss of jobs and so forth.
The taxes on cigars have been increased by $1 per thousand and since most cigars are now 10 cents and up, I do not think this will work any hardship on the cigar smokers. Then there is the tax on corporation income. There is no increase in taxation on small businesses with incomes of less than $25,000. However, there is an increase on incomes over this amount from 45 per cent to 47 per cent.
Surely no one will disagree with those increases in taxes which will increase the grants under compensating payments to the provinces of something like $162 million over 1956-57. Surely there is no one in this house who will disagree with the $160 million that will be required for the health insurance scheme with the participating provinces which all parties in this house have agreed to.
Then we have for straight health alone an increase of almost $30 million over 1956-57. There is also an expenditure of almost $20 million more in our resources department which will help to develop Canada, this great country of ours. Trans-Canada highway transportation is up around $45 million. No one can quarrel with this. Therefore I see no alternative to what the Minister of Finance has proposed to this house. If we are going to have these social security programs, if we are going to carry our share of the defence burdens, we must be prepared to pay for the same.
The Minister of Finance's proposals will not only meet these problems but will cut the deficit very substantially. Yet it will not interfere with normal recovery from a condition that has gradually built up over a period of years and must be corrected. I refer to the fact that we are now paying off some of the obligations incurred unwisely over the last decade. Let us look in brief retrospect at what happened.
Canada, a young and virile country, came out of the last war untouched and unscathed as far as her lands and industries were concerned. She occupied the third exporting position in the world but what do we find ten years later under a Liberal administration? Great Britain with half her industrial capacity ruined at the war's end, today more than challenges us in the quality of the goods produced and the cost per man-hour. Germany, almost in rubble after the last war, today in most fields can outsell us and beat us with respect to the cost per man-hour. Japan, a defeated, conquered nation, an occupied country, also challenges us and, in many cases, in spite of high tariffs, can outsell us on the spot in our own country.

The Budget-Mr. Rynard
This did not happen today; it happened over the period since the last war. Textile mills across Canada, one after another, had to close down until in 1957 there remained only a shadow of what once represented a great Canadian industry, close to the hearts of the people, because those industries were mostly located in the small cities and towns across Canada.
We saw this happen in the rubber footwear industry and in many other industries that I could mention. In the forestry industry we find Japan laying down mahogany, although facing heavy duties, and challenging British Columbia fir right on the very ground on which it is growing.
All three nations that I have mentioned are members of the Colombo group, nations that are, in large part, short of the raw materials they need to manufacture the finished articles which they have to sell in the markets of the world. They are obliged to depend on the import of those raw products which carry the price tag of labour costs in primary industry of the country from which they are imported. We in Canada sit on an abundance of almost every known raw material. What a tremendous advantage we should have over those other countries.
I have not said anything of the challenge of the U.S.S.R. in the economic field. Today we must face the economic challenge of a people who are looking forward to the day when they can outproduce the nations of the west, when they can outsell in the markets of the world those same nations. In some scientific fields today Russia is out far ahead of the free nations of the world. For example, the United States alone has three times the potential capacity for manufacture that Russia has. Where then is Canada's potential capacity going? Is it going into the manufacture of cars, television sets, radios and electric gadgets of all sorts? In this economic challenge, this challenge of our free way of life, it may be that some of this productivity must be channelled into increased productivity of goods that are needed for our defence or that are needed to increase new sciences or new methods which in turn will manufacture or be the means of manufacturing new products to sell in the markets of the world.
We in Canada, with the second highest standard of living in the world, with a country having some of the greatest resources in the world-which we did not place there- have we not become a little bit too demanding in our "keeping up with the Joneses"? Is it not a fact that over the past ten years we have been depleting some of those God-given natural resources and shipping them in payment for manufactured goods brought

into this country when we could have, in many cases, bought in Canada to support the factories and manufacturers of this country or factories could have been built to produce in this line? Over the past ten years, do not let us forget that we have piled up the largest trade deficit ever before piled up by this country. In this period of time it would appear to me that more should have been done and could have been done to protect and nurture more industry in this country.
In the immigration field all of us can recall the severe prodding that the administration at Ottawa took right after the war to fill in the wide-open spaces of this country and how slow they were to get started. It was not until one of the provinces, namely the province of Ontario under a Conservative government, undertook on its own to bring in the immigrants they needed that the Liberal party at Ottawa adopted some semblance of an immigration policy. Just let me refer to one point. These newcomers brought with them, in addition to their skills, over $800 million in cash and securities; another $300 million was brought in in personal belongings. They have bought or commenced thousands of small businesses across Canada. They have settled on thousands of farms, many of which were semi-vacant. What a golden opportunity the previous administration had and what a loss we have now suffered as a result of what appears to me to have been an extremely short-sighted policy. Today we are paying the interest on those mistakes. However, we must face the future. Today there is no standing still. We must compete or perish. New sciences, new techniques, new machines must be developed by the scientists and utilized by management of this country so that our costs per man-hour will be on a competitive basis in the markets of the world. That means the utilization of all man-power and of all available brain-power. The challenge must be met in the schools and universities, in industry, in labour. In the common people of this country there must be a clearer understanding of this challenge. We all either pull together or sink separately.
I am one of those who believe that the boys or girls growing up in Canada should be given the opportunity and encouragement to go as far as their ability will carry them. I am not one of those who believe that only the top students should be given the opportunity for study. The opportunity should be given to all of them. I have lived long enough to have seen some great contributions made by students who were in the lower half of their class. We must also remember that the more education given in our schools today, the better understanding there will be of democracy, and how to make that

democracy function at its best. Time is of the essence. The challenge is here.
Have we, as Canadians-all of us, in whatever field we find ourselves-the moral, spiritual and economic dedication to meet this challenge and surmount the problems in a country blessed with some of the richest resources in the world today, a country whose ancestors wrote into the history of yesterday the freedom that we enjoy today.
In closing, may I say this. May we as parliamentarians accept this challenge and dedicate ourselves to our task as examples to our fellow Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is almost five o'clock but since I probably would not get the unanimous consent of the house to adjourn the debate until eight o'clock, I suppose it is necessary for me to go on now for the ten minutes.
In rising to speak in this debate I want to refer to a speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in Vancouver on May 24. He said this and I hope he said it sincerely:
The Liberals say they cannot increase pensions and reduce taxes. Give us a chance and we will show you.
In December, 1957, we had a prologue to a show which promised a happy ending, and on Thursday night last we had the full second act of that show, which I think has ended in tragedy. I am sure all the provinces and municipalities of Canada are interested. The stage was all set, and we in this house sat in the pit and applauded the hero of the evening, who we hoped would bring a rabbit out of the hat. The hero entered. He was smiling but was without the blue boutonniere that he usually wears. He reached great heights in a soliloquy in his heroic role against that two-headed monster of debt and inflation. Most, but not all, applauded him when he went on to tell how much better he now intended to deal with this beast; but some of us here realized that in order to carry out even a fraction of his election promises he had still to beat this beast. The provinces and the people of Canada wondered how long this show must go on. I was struck the other night by one sentence of the minister in his speech on page 2424 of Hansard of April 9. He said:
With a good response to our Canada savings bond campaign this year, our net market borrowings in 1959-60 should be less than one-half of the $1,220 million borrowed in the market in 1958-59.
This was a master stroke to lull the public. There was no mention of the $1.35 billion that is coming due this year between July 1 and December 1. This must be refunded or dealt with in some other way by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). These people have to be sold again the new bonds, if the bonds
The Budget-Mr. McMillan are refunded, and we know that the interest rate has now risen to 5.06 per cent, according to table 48 in the budget papers. The market is waiting to see what happens. I think that is one reason the bonds have not gone up and might go down; in fact they have gone down somewhat in the last day or so. The minister needs close to $2.2 billion made up of next year's deficit borrowing for capital account plus the refunding of maturities due this year between July 1 and December 1. I realize that the Prime Minister can speak on the radio and tell little stories about patriotism and that the Minister of Finance can get a more modern version of the 1958 Fleming hat and have it advertised in every newspaper across the country. I expect a lot of these people will refund their bonds, likely at a higher interest rate.
Over and above this the minister has to deal, and deal constantly, with an amount of $1.6 billion approximately, which he has borrowed from time to time from the Bank of Canada or other banks in treasury bills.
I	know this has always been the practice, and therefore at the present time the minister is dealing at least with an amount between $3.7 billion and $3.8 billion. This is serious, and I think our country is in some rather deep financial trouble. I hope that the stage is not being set for the second Fleming folly.
What was there in the budget speech that the colleagues of the minister applauded so heartily the other night? I would say they applauded an increase in our gross public debt of $1.8 billion to the amount of $20.2 billion. That is in Hansard at table 2A. This represents an increase in debt of over $420 for every family of four in Canada. The minister's colleagues applauded that deficit of $835 million, made up of $617 million announced by the minister, plus $212 million taken out of the national defence equipment account, plus $6 million taken in fancy bookkeeping from an account which under section
II	of the National Defence Act represents surpluses from sales of national defence material. This deficit alone adds up pretty close to a debt of $200 for every family of four in Canada. They also warmly applauded another whopping deficit, and a major tax increase in spite of the prophecy that we would have a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product.
After all, there was very little else to applaud unless it be the largest spending in history, our largest peacetime deficit in history, the highest interest since the days of the Bennett government, the largest number ever of unemployed and, according to the Minister of Finance, the conversion loan was the greatest transaction in the

Private Bills
history of our country. Then we have also the highest interest paid in respect to current borrowings of treasury bills. The Minister of Finance seems to revel in superlatives, and if I were to use a superlative I would say that this is rather a mess, the greatest mess in our history. On page 2413 of Hansard the minister said:
Our net debt per capita was $847 ten years ago, $725 five years ago and is reduced to $676 now.
Surely in these words the minister is not trying to give anybody in Canada the idea that he has ever had anything to do with the reduction of debt. Of course, every baby born in Canada helps to spread the debt, not to reduce it as the minister infers. What a heavy extra load of debt he is handing to every newly born Canadian! The only unsolicited comment which I heard given the following morning by a man in Montreal concerning the budget was, "It took the Grits 22 years to get as unpopular as the Tories have in two."

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Boulanger for the second reading of Bill No. C-4, to amend the Financial Administration Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise at this time to speak to the bill before us which has been sponsored by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), my neighbour in this house. I am eager to have a vote taken on it. The bill has been discussed on various occasions in this chamber and we were enlightened by the contributions made by those hon. members who participated in the debate.
Before I resume my seat and request a vote on this bill I wish to make a few comments concerning bilingualism in relation to the constitution of Canada. It has been stated that bilingualism is not constitutional outside the province of Quebec. I intend to make reference to statements on the subject of the constitution of Canada written by some of the leading authorities on constitutional law.
The constitution of Canada, like that of many other countries including Great Britain, is based on two sets of rules. First, there are the rules of law which form that part of the constitution enforced by the courts. Second, there are the conventions of the constitution. These form what is known by the specialists as the morality of the constitution. These are the conventions that have grown up through usage and form the understandings, habits or practices which, though they may regulate the conduct of the several members of the sovereign power, of the ministry or of other officials, are not in reality laws at all since they are not enforced by the courts and do not appear on the statute books.
It has sometimes been stated in this house that bilingualism is not constitutional in Canada and because it has been stated by public men, various people throughout the country accept this remark and repeat it. In order to clarify the situation I shall read an extract from the book on constitutional law written by Dr. McCrea, former professor at the University of Toronto, volume 1, page 2. In paragraph 6 we find the following:
Rules of law and rules of convention-Among the rules relating to function a distinction has to be made between "rules of law" and "rules of convention." Rules of law are simply those rules of constitutional law which are enforced by the courts. Rules of convention, on the other hand, are rules of the constitution which are not enforced by the courts. Though regarded as part of "constitutional law," they are not law in the strict sense, but merely rules of constitutional usage or understanding which are enforced by public opinion only. It is with the "rules of law" of the constitution that the lawyer is concerned. The conventions of the constitution are matters which concern those engaged in public affairs rather than those engaged in the practice of law.

Mr. Speaker, in approaching this bill with its implications of bilingualism as introduced by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), my mind carries me back to the origin of this country. It was nearly 92 years ago that the father of the fathers of confederation, John A. Macdonald, with his able lieutenant Georges Etienne Cartier united behind their leadership a group of men of differing views but common purpose. This group of men became known as the fathers of confederation. They were men of vision, dedication and of faith.
After years of outstanding leadership, and hard work, coupled with compromise and diplomacy, a new nation was conceived. This new nation united two languages and two creeds and was dedicated to the principles of equality, opportunity, unity and freedom. It is to that country, no longer new, that we in this chamber stand dedicated and loyal today. We the members of this House of Commons, subscribe to those principles which were embodied in the creation of this country. We are proud to serve those principles.
Today we are considering a bill to establish that negotiable instruments of the government be printed in both the English and French languages. I am proud to say that I am in favour of this bill. I would be proud if this bill were to pass under this Conservative administration, because it was under a Conservative government that this country was united and that these two great races were united. It was under a Conservative government in 1934 that bilingual currency was introduced. It was under the present Conservative administration that a simultaneous translation system was introduced into this house. It would only be fitting if we were to progress further in the recognition of the partnership of these two great languages and pass this bill today.
Now, I should like to quote from the explanatory notes to this bill as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to provide that every cheque, draft, traveller's cheque, bill of exchange, postal note, money order, postal remittance and any other similar remittance of any department as defined in paragraph (f) of section 2 of the Financial Administration Act or of any crown corporation

enumerated in schedules B, C and D of the same act shall be printed in both the English and the French languages.
This is in accordance with the principle established in the Bank of Canada Act where it is enacted (subsection (4) of section 21) that the notes payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation in Canada issued by the bank shall be printed in both the official languages.
We can see that this principle has already been adopted and, as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) pointed out very ably, the principle of bilingualism is well established. It is questionable whether or not this legislation is necessary at all in order to enable the government to print these instruments in both French and English. We already have, as has been pointed out, bilingual currency, bilingual stamps, bilingual money orders and excise stamps. Certainly, bilingual cheques would be a natural progression.
I have a very great respect for bilingualism in this country. My only regret is that I am not more fluent myself in the French language. According to the 1951 census only 8.5 per cent of the population of Manitoba were of French origin. I would say that there is no higher percentage than that in my own constituency.
