speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in debating the purposes sought to be achieved by legislation which would require the printing in the two main languages of Canada of all the negotiable instruments issued by the Canadian government and its agencies I believe that we as members of parliament must have regard to the spirit which reflects the desire to have this type of legislation put through, and it is to my mind a matter as much of the heart as it is of the head. My constituents are not directly affected by this proposed legislation. Not more than 50 of the 200,000 people in my constituency speak normally in the French language, yet I am one of those who believes that this country in the nationhood we now share achieved that nationhood and will continue to prosper and flower only as we have regard each to the other, and that without those things of the spirit and the heart there would have been no possibility of nationhood. Indeed, in its beginnings it might have taken the form of other nations, one of them not at all removed and which achieved the beginnings of nationhood in the fires of civil commotion. We in this country achieved nationhood by the joining together primarily of two great lingual and ethnic groups. I am one of those who believes that there is no

The Budget-Mr. McMillan such thing as a French Canadian, nor is there any such thing as an English Canadian. There are French speaking Canadians and English speaking Canadians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext: What is the difference?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR PRINTING OF NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS IN BOTH ENGLISH AND FRENCH
speechtext:
What is the difference? There is a great difference. The difference comes in the adjectival use of "French speaking". A French Canadian is not the same thing as a French speaking Canadian. I would be delighted to have the hon. member join us at dinner when some of the 55 Conservative members from Quebec will be glad to enlighten him as to the difference.
This sense of spirit seems to me to inhabit the one objection which could legally be made to this legislation, and that is in section 133 of the British North America Act. It is sometimes said that section 133 places a proscription, a limit, upon the use in official communications and official assemblies of the two languages. Section 133 requires that English and French are equally usable in the parliament of Canada, in its journals and its papers, and in pleading before any court established under that act. But I believe that section 133 of the British North America Act was intended to set the minimal standard for the use of the two languages, and I, as an English speaking Canadian, think the criterion, whether the principle of this bill merits our support, must be decided in the first instance by the French speaking members. If they have perhaps a minority feeling toward this legislation, and if they ask parliament for this legislation, then I think that their request should be taken by us as a guide to our conduct, for certainly nothing that we do should be inclined to retard or diminish the sense of the spirit which was achieved by the mingling of these two ethnic groups.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was interrupted at five o'clock I was


proceeding to speak about how much this government has cost the people of Canada this year. Previously I had stated that this government, taking into consideration the depletion in the unemployment insurance fund, would cost the taxpayers of Canada over $1 billion this year. It has exceeded that amount; indeed, the figure of expenditure runs to $1.07 billion. This amount represents overspending. In the financial planning of the government it has built up increased charges which will be carried into future budgets and result in overspending in future years.
This overspending amounts to approximately $3 million a day, or $125,000 an hour. As I have stated before, that daily expenditure is about equivalent to the assessment of a town with a population of from 3,000 to 5,000. It means that the equivalent of the value of a $10,000 farm goes down the drain in overspending every 4J minutes.
I know that the government has saved a lot of money this year in cutting down defence expenditures. I also know that military leaders in Great Britain, the United States and even our own Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) have stated that we need manned interceptors. We were informed that the Arrow would go to 3 times as fast as the interceptors now in use, but we were also told that those now in use would suffice at the present time. Even at that the minister admitted they would not overtake the modern bombers. I should like to know what protection we in this country have with manned interceptors? In my opinion what we have does not amount to adequate protection. I hope that the safety of our people has not been jeopardized in order to meet election promises.
I am not sufficiently well informed to know whether our course in dispensing with the Arrow was a proper one or not but I do know there has been a saving of many millions of dollars in reduced defence expenditures. The former government spent a great deal more of the tax dollar in defence and certainly if this government were putting the same proportion of the tax dollar into defence its deficit would be considerably larger than it is. The Canadian air vice-marshal has said we need the Arrow. I have seen or heard no reasonable argument to the contrary. I am not saying this government made a wrong decision but it failed to present us with any technical reasons in support of the course it followed. The voice of the one man who should know was heard but once and never heard again. I cannot help but feel that a select committee made up of hon. members from all parties in this house should have had an opportunity to hear him and others giving

expert opinions. In that way the Canadian people would have had confidence in the safety of this country. They would know that the decision was made purely for military and not for political reasons.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in referring to the conversion loan described it as a huge success when in fact we on this side of the house think it was the biggest flop in the financial history of this country. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) said yesterday that we are paying about $345 million more in extra interest up to the time of the original due dates of the 6th to 9th victory loan series. The minister does not come by $345 million very easily. In fact, that would be a whopping deficit in a budget for one year.
In referring to the financial policy followed last year, as reported at page 2415 of Hansard of April 9, 1959, the Minister of Finance said:
I think nearly all informed observers have agreed that our policy last year was right in its direction and about right in its degree.
I believe that is utter trash. The people of Canada will not believe this. Nearly every daily paper, periodical, financial paper and other publications carried frequent articles written by bank presidents, heads of trust companies and other financial institutions, as well as statements by financial writers, giving advice to the minister, imploring him to set an example in government by sane financing and spending. Every hon. member of this house knows this to be true. Indeed, almost everybody in Canada knows this to be true and I do not need to verify it by quotations so many of which are available in the recent press.
In my opinion the Minister of Finance tries to smooth everything over to his own advantage. In referring to the conversion loan in the budget speech, as reported at page 2411 of Hansard, the minister had this to say:
But in so far as the market and the investor were concerned, this $61 billion was not spread over eight years, because the first four of the issues were callable in 1959 or earlier and the 1966 issue was callable at any time after September 1, 1961. From the investors' point of view, therefore, this $61 billion had to be considered as being spread over, not eight years but approximately three years.
Who is the minister trying to fool? The bonds were callable only at the option of the government. No bond holder would lie awake wondering where he might reinvest the money obtained from the redemption of any bonds this government, plunging into debt, might call in. I wonder if this gave the minister the idea of committing the Canadian taxpayer to long term non-callable loans? The foolish conversion loan contributed more than anything else to the unsettling of our bond
The Budget

Mr. McMillan market and served to push interest rates up. When people saw such inept financing many got their cash for converted victory bonds right away before the market started its precipitous decline. I personally know some who did that.
Even the Minister of Finance was prompted to say in the budget debate, as reported at page 2415:
But the fact remains that the Canadian bond market has not been accustomed to absorbing as large a volume of new government bonds of Canada as we have had to offer during the past year. The impact of our borrowings, which over the year as a whole have been achieved largely in a non-inflationary manner, has exerted an upward pressure on interest rates.
I think this is really a confession at last that what the Minister of Finance did was to push the bond interest upward. Members on this side of the house told him what would happen. I myself told him what would happen. We told him that he would be stopped in his tracks. On January 21, in the debate on the speech from the throne I said, as reported at page 168 of Hansard:
A banker lends money to a creditor if the manager thinks he is a good risk; but if he becomes a spendthrift or otherwise shows that he cannot handle his money wisely the credit is withdrawn. This is exactly what the people of Canada have done to the Minister of Finance. They have called a halt to his wild spending by refusing to bu,y his bonds at the fast rate he requires. It is just as simple as that, no matter how much the Minister of Finance confuses us with such terms as bank rate, bills of exchange rate, short and long term money rates, and so on.
It is quite evident from what I put on the record before five o'clock that a lot of the borrowing last year was only short term borrowing, and we know that nearly $1.35 billion comes due this year between July 1 and December 1. Hon. members will recall that between 1959 and 1966, $6.4 billion in the 5th to the 9th victory loans were to come due. Almost 55 per cent of those victory loans were sold in the long term issues, but slightly over 45 per cent of them were either not sold or else were sold as short term issues, and those two short term issues are due in 1961 and 1965 at an earlier date than many of the original victory loan bonds. For the latter bonds to which I have referred, namely the short term issues, the minister will pay an extra total interest bill of some $66.5 million, plus millions in bonuses and commissions for a very questionable advantage because one-half of them must again be dealt with by the Minister of Finance during this parliament. The minister again will have a big bill for refinancing the maturities over again, with another bil bill in commissions, advertising and what not. This is the same

The Budget-Mr. McMillan minister who used to talk about the former government and their waste and extravagance.
The main advantage in the conversion that we have got at the present time is that we have 55 per cent of the bonds for a longer term; but to get 55 per cent over to a longer term we have paid a terrible price. We paid $71 million in costs, plus increased yearly interest charges of $66 million a year. This latter figure includes $7 million the minister reported as a yearly amount to amortize the cost of the loan. Hon. members will see that the minister got rid of only a little over half of the victory loan bonds into longer maturities, and he has the rest of them very much with him at the present time.
If the minister had dealt with the 5th victory loan bonds as they came due in the normal way there would not have been the same upward pressure on interest rates, and certainly he could have sold them or could have refunded them, probably at a better price and certainly not at any higher price than the average of 4 per cent, the interest that he had to pay on the conversion issue. Had he done this he would have saved over $50 million this year alone. This amount is about double the increase in personal income tax, or at least $10 million more than the increased personal contributions to the old age pension fund for this year alone, and it would be many millions more than the increased taxes on cigars and cigarettes and the increased taxes on women's cosmetics which are being imposed by this budget. I think this Fleming folly will be felt by generations of Canadians probably yet unborn.
This promise that the conversion loan would make money more readily available to the municipalities and to the provinces at a cheaper rate is simply not true. Hon. members here have only to ask their bankers or their municipalities what they think of this and I do not think they would find anyone to agree with it.
At the present time many municipalities have money borrowed from the bank. There are municipalities in the Niagara district which have borrowed money and have loans at the bank which they cannot get out at a reasonable debenture rate. Canadian government bonds became a glut on the market. They fell in price and put the price of money up to everybody. The people in many of the remotest parts of Canada will be paying extra interest for their sewers, sidewalks and roads long after the minister has retired with his foolish and misguided fiscal policy.
Our bonds are lower and therefore money is costing us more than it is costing most other countries of the western free world, including such countries as Belgium, Norway,

Sweden and even revolutionary Cuba, whose long term bonds are selling well above ours right now. In fact, our bonds do not seem to be wanted in New York or in other world markets. Sometime ago I quoted that one Canadian bond was sold in New York when over $375,000 worth of Australian bonds were sold that week. In the week before last there was not one Canadian bond sold on that market, and last week all those that were sold were bonds that went down in price over their previous sale, while bonds of most other countries of the western free world were going up.
It was put on record in the British House of Commons and by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) here that Canada has the highest unemployment, along with Italy, percentage-wise in relation to working forces of most other countries of the western free world. I think our high interest rates go along with the high unemployment rate. I submit that the municipalities, the provinces and individuals cannot borrow money at those high rates and cannot proceed with projects that they would like to proceed with at this time, which would take up a lot of the slack of unemployment.
I do not think the minister is doing anything to lower interest rates. We all know that in February he sold $200 million worth of bonds in two issues, one was a 2} per cent issue and the other a 3 per cent issue, and they were sold in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $25,000, $100,000 and $1 million. As I said before, those bonds were not for the little man and the minister rather took exception to that. I say that if any little man had $1,000 he had to be pretty nimble and agile to get one of those bonds in the 15 minutes in which the books were open.
How does the minister expect the ordinary people to buy bonds under such circumstances? If we refer to table 48 we will see it shows that the yield at the price to the government of the 3 per cent bonds due in December, 1960 was 5.06 per cent, the highest price since the days of the Bennett government. The other issue was a 2f per cent, 13-month bond, which cost the government 4.86 per cent. They both carried income tax gimmicks which cost our treasury well over 6 per cent net when sold to big corporations and others in the 50 per cent income tax bracket.
Instead of trying to cut expenditures the government is establishing a record of expenditures year after year. The minister used to blame the former government for waste and extravagance based on the number of civil servants employed. At the end

of the first year in office of the present government the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said that there were 8,124 more civil servants on June 30, 1958 than the previous June, and with about two and a half months to go I suppose we will have another increase of the same size. According to the book of main estimates, the Minister of Finance has 143 more civil servants in his own department than his predecessor had. In that connection may I say that the only thing of greater magnitude with which they have to deal is debt.
I want to say again that a fundamental weakness in the Bank of Canada is the fact that the government has appointed some highly political men to the board of directors of that bank. They should be above reproach just like our judiciary as their decisions influence the lives of all Canadians. Are we assured that their decisions are free from political considerations and are for the good of Canada?
When I see our bonds selling on the world markets below those of Cuba which is in a state of revolution, I wonder, and so do many other Canadians wonder. No wonder our Canadian bonds are selling on a par with or lower than many of our provincial bonds including many provincial guaranteed bonds. I put that on the record in the house not long ago. The ordinary people will not buy long term government bonds unless they have a guarantee as to principal at all times. They have been jockeyed out of buying these high interest, short term bonds but they will be let in to pay for these bonds and to help pay for the mistakes of the government.
The minister is often evasive and we can only find the true figures in the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada and in other places or we have to work them out ourselves. He tells us regularly that our mathematics are wrong but in Toronto before the Canadian club he said:
The average coupon rate of the bonds converted is now 3.83 per cent.
He was referring to the conversion loan. Without taking into consideration the numbers of bonds sold in each category, the minister added together the percentages, 3 plus 3f plus 4J plus 4J and divided by 4. That seems like a childish way. He arrived at 3.83 but afterwards he admitted that it should be 4 per cent.
Again, when I asked him if the figures he gave in that address in Toronto were right he said that he did not know what figures I was referring to but if he gave them they were right. Here again, when pressed further he admitted he had understated the increased 66968-9-171
The Budget-Mr. McMillan interest as a result of conversion by $10 million. I regard these as mistakes but there are other errors in statements made by the minister, always made in favour of the government, that I regard more seriously.
On February 13, 1958, the minister spoke to the Empire club in Toronto about government bonds being immediately oversubscribed and went on to say:
The twelfth Canada savings bond campaign was Inaugurated in October and achieved a record response. The offering was discontinued at December 31. By that time a record of gross sales of $1,175 billion had been achieved, vastly exceeding the amount realized on any previous issue.
This seems to me a most spurious deception because the amount of Canada savings bonds in the hands of the public increased only by $436 million between October 1 and December 31 and not by $1,175 billion in that period as you might be led to expect. I understand that what happened was that people turned in some $700 million of less desirable Canada savings bonds for more desirable bonds, but on the other hand that is not what you are led to believe when you read the statement of the minister.
The minister said in his budget speech last year, concerning the government's cash requirements and the loan which it had floated in April, as found at page 1241 of Hansard for June 17, 1958:
We have already made a good beginning. Since April 1 we have sold issues totalling $950 million, of which $350 million was new cash.
You will get some idea about the minister's expression, "a good beginning," if you read the remarks of the governor of the Bank of Canada on page 5 of his annual report where he says:
There were two periods of large scale monetary expansion. The first took place at the time of the May 1 new issue of government securities when it appeared that a net increase in non-bank holdings could not be achieved.
I want you to mark those words, "could not be achieved," because we were certainly led to believe that these bonds were going over like hotcakes. When the minister tabled the 1959-60 estimates he said, as found at page 705 of Hansard of February 5:
The most noteworthy feature is that compared with those for the present year, 1958-59, these estimates provide for a decrease of $39.1 million in the non-statutory items.
I do not know whom the minister thinks he is fooling. This may read well in the press but the minister does not compare like with like. What he has done is to compare this year's main estimates with last year's main estimates plus supplementary estimates plus further supplementary estimates Nos. 1 and 2, and last year these supplementaries

The Budget-Mr. McMillan amounted to $427.5 million. The main estimates this year are $416 million greater than the main estimates last year and we are bound to have supplementary estimates this year as we have had every year since I have been a member of the house.
If we question the minister's figures we are told by him that we are irresponsible or that we are lacking in our knowledge of mathematics. The minister himself has not shown himself to be infallible in mathematics. The finding of the $10 million mistake in connection with the increased interest with respect to the conversion loan, together with many other mistakes with respect to statements made by the minister, all made to the advantage of the government and either planned or by misadventure, requires a good deal of laborious work. It involves going to statistical reports of the Bank of Canada and other publications, checking and crosschecking, and in some cases it requires endless calculations particularly in arriving at interest rates.
If the minister continues to give us information at variance with subsequent reports we will have no time to do this work since we have so many committee meetings to attend and we want to fulfil our responsibilities to the people of Canada. We are willing to overlook honest mistakes on the part of the minister and we have and we realize that the government has got to defend the decisions that are made. But we take serious objection to statements that mislead the country and mislead members of the house. Such statements may give the government temporary advantage but after a time all factual statements become suspect. I have given three examples and I have many more before me. I should like to think of all ministers of the crown as being straightforward and not misleading in their statements, and I should like to make an appeal to the Minister of Finance to be factual in his statements in the future. Is my time up?

I want to say a few words on trade. If we had more trade we would not have so much unemployment. Back in the good old days when we used to have nearly 100 per cent employment 20 per cent of our people depended for their livelihood on our foreign trade. This government seems to blow hot and cold with our best customer, the United States.
Now, at election time there were criticisms from almost every Tory platform and in the Tory press about certain aspects of United States capital coming into Canada. Then we had the great talk about the diversion of trade and again great pronouncements by the

Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) about preserving our sovereignty in the north, clearly directed against the United States forces situated along the D.E.W. line and other bases up there.
Now, what has happened? On March 9 our government sold gas and exploration rights on nearly three million acres in northern Canada. Who got these rights? Canadian corporations got 4 per cent; British, United States and Canadian corporations got 3 per cent and United States corporations got 93 per cent, of which Canadian subsidiaries of American companies got 25 per cent.

Without that increase, the future of this country would have been seriously jeopardized and we would have had to wage an even more bitter fight against inflation, that economic disease which we must face and check in the best interests of Canada.
The sole purpose of my remarks is to show how, with the problems facing the government, there could not be in a general way, a more effective solution to develop our trade relations and to meet existing problems.
All hon. members know that Canada is one of the great trading powers of the world, that our country, with its sparse population and its diversified natural wealth, has to seek foreign markets for many of its products. Farm and forest products would soon remind us of the fact if ever we were inclined to forget it. It is true that the manufactured products' sector of our economy has developed considerably in the last 15 years, but there again the need to export to foreign markets is being felt. Need I refer to our large sales of wheat, newsprint and lumber?
The danger which threatened our international trade was the exaggerated increase
66968-9-171J
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche of our trade with our good neighbours to the south. Of course, they are our best customers and it would be wrong not to consider them as such. On the other hand it would be a great mistake on our part- and that is what the present government has fully realized-to neglect our commercial outlets within the commonwealth, and in other countries of the free world, which enable us to protect the stability of our trade and to ensure, as much as possible, a favourable trade balance with more countries.
This quest for a balance in our international trade, which was one of the main purposes of the commercial and economic commonwealth conference, held in Montreal last fall, proved to be most fruitful.
Hon. members will no doubt remember what the hon. Minister of Finance stated last Thursday, in that connection:
The results of the Conference fully justified its opening theme: "An expanding Commonwealth in an expanding world".
That policy is strictly a policy of the present government. Outlined on several occasions by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), it was summarized here in the house by the hon. Minister of Finance on June 17, 1958 as follows:
In brief, they may be described as follows:
1.	To achieve expansion, diversification, better balance and greater stability in our trade with all countries;
2.	To extend and strengthen Canada's trade and economic relationships with the commonwealth;
3.	To support and promote a regime of iaw, order and morality in the field of international trade; to respect the spirit and intent of international commitments; and to stand ready to defend our rights and interests if they are challenged or ignored;
4.	To recognize the legitimate needs of Canadian producers; and to safeguard them against unfair trading practices;
5.	To promote the balanced growth of all sectors of Canadian industry and agriculture.
Despite the government's efforts in the field of international trade, the economic slump, which spared none of the western powers, has had such an impact that Canada was faced with domestic difficulties, foremost of which, without doubt, was the shortage of jobs.
As you are well aware, Canada has great obligations, both on the international front and on the national front, which must be met. It has the obligation to protect its citizens in a world where scientific discoveries become obsolete overnight; it has to provide social security for Canadian citizens; it has to help provide a living for its people.

The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche
We are now enjoying a period of peace, a peace not altogether free from fear and anxiety, but peace none the less. And we have to remain prepared for any emergency. That is why the government is doing all it can to share in common defense with the western powers, so as to give Canada adequate protection.
Social security is costly, but within the limits set by justice and charity, it is a task of paramount importance. There is no need for me to mention here old age pensions, increased unemployment insurance benefits, and all the other social security measures that exist for the welfare of Canadians.
The government did not hesitate, despite increased unemployment insurance benefits and other legislative amendments, to set its sights as the hon. Minister of Finance stated last year, not on a balanced budget, but on providing jobs for the unemployed. That is why some $250 million were made available this year for housing construction, why the public works program was stepped up, why co-operation was extended to the provinces and municipalities for winter works, etc.
The economic recovery is gaining strength. Everywhere, business activity is picking up. Surely, the best yardstick of this is that mentioned by the hon. Minister of Finance when he drew attention in this house to the reduced number of unemployed as compared with last year, while indicating that the country's labour force has increased by 152,000 workers. Moreover, the economy of free countries is improving, which means that international trade stands to gain by this.
While it is true that universal consent, in itself, is not a valid argument, it is a strange thing that several countries of the world, with a free economy, have thought fit to resort to methods similar to those used by this government to solve their economic and financial problems. Thus in the grave crisis facing France, the drastic remedies applied by General de Gaulle's administration are apparently the only way to ensure economic recovery. Far be it from me to compare Canada's economy with that of France. Canada is going through a period of sustained economic development unequalled in its history.
If we take a look at a country whose economy is strangely similar to ours, namely the United States, we find that the Eisenhower administration has submitted a budget involving the extension of a special 52 per cent tax on corporate profits, as well as other taxes on such items as cars, alcoholic beverages and tobacco, which normally were to be withdrawn next June 30. Moreover, Mr. Eisenhower recommended an increase in the excise tax on automobile and aircraft fuels, as well as drastic measures to raise the yield of the tax on life insurance companies, so as to reach the co-operatives.
Many people feel that only an effort such as this, to balance in some degree the budget of the American nation, will ensure monetary stability. Otherwise, we might perhaps expect financial and economic chaos.
In the state of New York, the new governor, Mr. Rockefeller, inaugurated his term by imposing new taxation, including a tax on personal income, in order to put some order into government finance. The day after he brought down his budget, on February 3, 1959, the New York Times concluded its leading editorial with these words:
Governor Rockefeller chose an unpleasant and perhaps unpopular policy which, however, was certainly dictated by common sense. It would have been dangerous for us and for the economy of the state if he had not stopped the drifting of public finance towards bankruptcy. He could hardly do less if he wanted to put the state on a sound basis. He probably could not do any better in any case, politically speaking, at the present time. We congratulate him again for his courage.
Speaking generally about the problem of the public debt in The Canadian Banker (winter issue of 1958) E. P. Neufeld wrote the following:
While we must acknowledge that government expenditures are rather rigid and that the government has to be financed one way or another, successful management of the debt will only be possible, without inflationary prices, if the authorities allow the interest rate to develop freely toward high levels and if federal taxation is increased.
In other words, it is impossible to avoid inflation and its disastrous consequences without resorting to some rather drastic measures, and especially to increased taxation.
Besides, we have seen many instances recently of public administrations having to resort to increased taxation to ensure the development of the country without allowing inflation to jeopardize the future of the nation.
In this regard, the Minister of Finance had this to say, as found at page 2408 of Hansard of April 9, 1959:
I do not see any present evidence of overt inflation in the coming year, in fact the consumer

price index has declined for the past four consecutive months. We must, however, continue on guard against potential inflationary pressures. I believe that is well within the power of Canadians to achieve reasonable price stability without sacrificing either immediate recovery or balanced growth.
Can anyone seriously point an accusing finger at this government and charge it with failure to accept its responsibilities in the face of the complex problems of our trade and social security policies and of the economic recession?
We did all that could be done. Of course, our methods can be questioned, but who could say that the methods suggested by the opposition would have given better results? Unfounded assertions and theories offering no possibility of direct application are mere dreams and the fruit of questionable mental gymnastics.
During the last war, we had many budgets showing a deficit. We were in a state of emergency. We are now going through another rather difficult period. It takes money to ward off an economic slump and an employment crisis. Every Canadian citizen knows that the government has to take such action as is necessary to secure the revenues that will enable it to take care of those in greatest need, and to work toward the recovery of the Canadian economic life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join those who have preceded me in this debate and offer a word of appreciation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the monumental-with the help of his assistants-job of preparing and presenting the budget which in itself constitutes a project of major proportions.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) for the very careful and critical analysis of the weak features of the budget. The minister's statement that the budget must be flexible to meet changing conditions and changes in the economic condition of the country is a statement with which I fully agree. His statement with regard to inflation, however, is a horse of another kind.
I am afraid inflation is still very much with us, although I wish it were not so. But the fact is that most commodities cost more. In the building of a small home the cost has gone up from 5 per cent to 10 per cent. The effect of the freight rate increases alone raised the price of an ordinary dwelling
The Budget-Mr. Badanai in Fort William by $200. If there are no adjustments made in this field the cost of every commodity, including food, will go up. The trend of rising costs will continue, which only means inflation. On this occasion I again appeal to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to give serious consideration to the proposal which I made on April 7 last regarding the adjustment of freight rates throughout northwestern Ontario.
The Minister of Finance argued that inflation is not inevitable. Perhaps it could be curbed if the proper measures were applied at the right moment. I am not saying that this is an easy matter which can be resolved with a stroke of a pen. It is something which requires deep study and political courage. However, if we are faced with a choice of inflation or unemployment, of the two evils inflation would be the lesser. I have here a short quotation from the Labour Gazette. It states:
Nobody has a formula for dealing with inflation and unemployment at one and the same time. A number of business leaders seem to think inflation the graver threat of the two, perhaps they are right.
"But no cure is any good that tries to make inflation better by making unemployment worse, and treats a sound dollar as if it were more important than a sound man."
In order to combat both these evils it is necessary to overhaul government thinking on the matter of trade. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) mentioned trade but was unable to finish his speech because his time was up. But how can we hope to expand trade with other nations when the government is extending their protectionistic tendencies, which are traditional, of course, with the Conservative party?
Mr. Hector McKinnon, a recognized authority on tariffs, has recently stated that the time is now opportune for greater flexibility in GATT to provide for faster readjustment in fixed rates. He also urged a custom union or free trade pact with the United States.

In the constituency I represent there are some very fine dairy and truck garden farms. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the debate which follows the presentation of the budget, hon. members are usually given great latitude in their choice of subjects. I, therefore, wish to place before this house tonight four subjects, three of which are domestic in nature and the fourth, while national in concept, has international ramifications.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) concluded his budget speech the other day with this statement, as found on page 2425 of Hansard for April, 1959:
Canada has no reason for fear. Blessed as she has been by a benign Providence above all other lands, she can face her shining future with utmost confidence.
[Mr. Badanai.l

As one who is part of a group of Canadians who have the greatest part of their lives still ahead of them, and as one who would, therefore, most benefit or suffer from the actions of our leaders, may I say I share that spirit of confidence. Looking into the future I can conceive that it is quite possible that Canada will develop into the most influential nation within the commonwealth. It is entirely possible that this development will take place within my lifetime. It is a prospect that is at once exciting and one which fires the imagination. So I am proud to have the privilege of serving Canada at a time when so much remains to be done.
However, because so much remains to be done I feel that at times we Canadians are too immersed with details and problems of our day-to-day existence that we sometimes forget to look at the over-all picture. I can think of no better time than now to pause and to consider our future position. Our country today is in a period of transition. We are experiencing a feeling of restlessness. These conditions have been brought about by national and international events of serious proportions. Nationally we have an economic situation that baffles the experts because, on the one hand, we have a level of high prosperity and, on the other, we have a level of high unemployment.
Internationally, the Berlin situation, the unrest in the countries of Africa and Asia, the challenge of communism and the threat of a nuclear war, all have given our leaders serious concern, as indeed they have to most men. These are common difficulties faced by almost every other country. But it is useless, I submit, to talk about what other countries are doing unless we ourselves are prepared to think about these problems. In this connection, I would remind the house that our leaders are engaged in trying to find solutions to these very vexing problems. They would be the first to admit that these are serious problems. While this party has done a great deal for this country in the short time it has formed the government, I know that this government will do even more in the future.
But how we develop and in what direction will depend upon what the people of Canada want. To say that we want Canada to develop into a great nation is trite. I suggest that our consideration should be, how much are we willing to sacrifice to help our country develop into a great nation. As in all things, without a clear knowledge of what we want, and without a desire and ambition to work for a common goal, all our dreams and hopes are for nothing. As a young person I have a great stake in the future of this country. As I said earlier, it is not

at all impossible that within my lifetime Canada will become the leading nation within the commonwealth. How are we going to achieve that position? One answer that I can give is the answer given by our leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
In the first place, there must be a vision of our future greatness. There is a biblical saying that without vision the people perish. In the second place, there must be confidence in our own ability and this confidence must spring from a realistic appraisal of our own capacities. Third, there must be a willingness to work hard. These three requirements imply that there must be an orderly and controlled development of our resources. We must guard against too rapid an expansion of our resources, otherwise there will not be the maximum and most efficient utilization of these resources. There must be a controlled development to ensure that it is our country, and every segment within our country, which receives the prime benefit of our resources. There must also be an increase in our population because an increased population means an increased demand for goods and services which, in turn, stimulates production. One result of our present small population is that our producers, in trying to reduce costs, must try to sell our goods overseas, and it is in this field of international trade that we have our most serious problem because we compete with countries who can produce the same goods at a lower cost.
The ramifications of that situation are obvious. None the less, Canada is taking her place industrially in the world. In taking our place we are facing the economic facts of life which industrial giants like the United States of America and Great Britain experienced long ago. We must now have an economic shakedown in which we will gradually gear our activities and our production to our resources.
Such a period of adaptation is difficult at the best of times, but it is aggravated by our high cost economy and by the entry of the U.S.S.R. and communist China into the field of international trade. The Prime Minister underlined the seriousness of the situation when he spoke in the house on January 19. As reported at page 55 of Hansard he said this:
-there is an offensive in trade that is bound to be one of the most challenging dangers of the days ahead.
The communists have declared economic war on us. Whether or not we can survive will depend upon our ability to meet their competition. All this calls for a mature and realistic appraisal of our obligations. In this connection I suggest that government, management 66968-9-1721
The Budget-Mr. Jung
and labour must take time for deliberation and co-operation. Failure to do this will result in our way of life being overwhelmed without one shot being fired.
I think that one of the greatest tasks facing government, business and labour is to embark upon a program of education so that everyone will clearly understand and appreciate the magnitude of the economic war which has been declared against us by the communist countries. In these communist countries there is a continuing process of education. You can call it propaganda or indoctrination or what you will; but there is a program aimed at telling their people again and again what is their goal. We must admit that they can see the results of their planning. We in the free world have nothing comparable because we have been brought up in an atmosphere of plenty. We cannot conceive that, materially at least, things could be better. The other countries have a sense of urgency because they see our material accomplishments and so their goal is not only to equal us but also to surpass us. This economic competition is competition in the fullest sense of the word, and there is no prize at the end but merely survival. This then is the responsibility facing Canadians. As for myself, I am confident that we can survive and prosper. We have the means and the technical knowledge, although in the light of sputnik I have some reservations even on that thought.
In meeting this challenge we must not forget to help the underdeveloped countries because in helping them we help ourselves. I have heard some people criticize the grants which we make to the Colombo plan because they say that charity should begin at home. Mr. Speaker, may I say that it does begin at home because practically all the money which we give to the Colombo plan in order to help these underdeveloped countries is used by them to buy Canadian goods and services. They do not use this money in order to buy things from other countries. So let there be no misunderstanding about the way in which that money is spent. Not only do we in Canada benefit from supplying goods and services to these countries but also we receive their friendship and good will. This friendship and good will is all important, because in the conflict of ideologies which faces us today we are trying to sell our way of life to other countries. However, the bargain counter days of democracy are over. No longer do we see countries rushing to embrace our way of life which is on display before highly critical buyers who are getting increasingly harder and harder to convince that our way of life is in fact the best way of life.
We seem to think that just because another country lives in the same century as we do

The Budget-Mr. Jung they should acknowledge the superiority of our way of life, and at times we are bewildered and even angered when our overtures to them are rebuffed. We fail to appreciate their culture and outlook which they have developed over many thousands of years, and in exasperation we throw up our hands and say "We cannot understand them". Of course we cannot understand them because we try to look at them through our own eyes and through our own experiences rather than through theirs. Only when we can look at them through their eyes can we begin to understand and appreciate the differences between us.
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, I spoke about the responsibilities of government, business and labour in co-operating to meet the economic challenge of the communists. How should we go about this task? I suggest the establishing of an organization which will include not only government, business and labour but also representatives of the press. In the economic education of the Canadian people I feel that the press, with all its related media, is the only way in which the man in the street can become acquainted with the facts of this economic struggle. We have as separate organizations government agencies, business groups and labour unions; but I feel that there should be even more cohesive groups working with and not against each other. These groups should be not merely concerned with getting an increase in salaries or in asking the workers to produce more. It is my opinion that once the facts of this economic struggle have been brought before the Canadian people they will be willing to make the necessary sacrifices. It is useless to ask people to do something unless you explain to them the reason why they do it.
Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, the example which the Prime Minister gave to this house after his visit to Asia. He said that cloth which is manufactured in Great Britain and which sells for $1 a yard in Asia is produced and sold by the Japanese for 60 cents a yard, but communist China produces and sells the same thing for 33 cents a yard. But according to other reports, underselling applies not only to cloth but also to things like sewing machines, cement, nails, bicycles, canned fruit, vacuum jugs, electric fans, typewriters, radios, caustic soda, paper, glass, ceramics and some machinery. Reflect for a moment, Mr. Speaker, and you will realize that these items, while insignificant in themselves, are in great demand in the countries of southeast Asia which are beginning to raise their standards of living.
In the composition of this organization which I propose to call the Canada trade council, for want of a better name, I should


like to see more rank and file members of labour organizations included because, in the final analysis, they are the ones who will have to produce more and make the most sacrifices. I would even suggest that the government arrange for such a group to visit communist countries in order to see for themselves what is our competition. The few industrialists who have visited communist China and the U.S.S.R., for axample, have returned deeply impressed and indeed deeply frightened by the great advances which they have seen in technology. It is the boast of Premier Krushchev that by 1967 Russia will be the world's greatest producer. From the information which is available that appears to be no idle boast. Only yesterday a United press item from Moscow said this:
Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev's drastic sevenyear plan for catching up with U.S. industrial output over-fulfilled ts first targets by 105 per cent, the government announced today.
This idea of a Canada trade council, is a subject which I said had international ramifications, even though it was national in concept, because this council could be expanded to include all members of the commonwealth. Hon. members will recall the commonwealth trade and economic conference which was held in Montreal last September. The theme was an expanding commonwealth in an expanding world. This theme was singularly appropriate, but I suggest that there should be greater continuity in thought and coordination in action beyond the commonwealth. The idea of a national trade council, designed to educate the people of each country within the commonwealth to the urgent necessity of meeting this communist trade offensive, could, if projected to the international level, provide the driving force to maintain the momentum of the decisions taken at the commonwealth trade and economic conference. Without a larger goal, without a more urgent purpose, trade conferences could become bogged down with national restrictions and considerations. I cannot express too strongly my concern for the need for this economic education, because in the end it is education for freedom.
I have already spoken about the need for an orderly and controlled development of our resources. One of the greatest resources of any country is its people, and so I wish to deal with my other three subjects. These are university students, old age pensioners and housing.
Under the British North America Act education is the responsibility of the provincial authorities. On the other hand, nine out of the ten provinces have received grants from the federal treasury for education. In spite of the efforts of provincial and federal authorities our school facilities and standards

are according to reports way behind those of the U.S.S.R. Universities are plagued by a shortage of money, and many are operating at large deficits. To offset these deficits fees have been increased, but these increases have added to the hardships of the students. I do not think everyone is entitled to a university education, even if he can afford it. My concern is for the deserving student who cannot afford to attend university. I know that local scholarships and grants are available, but many of these are insufficient in themselves for the undergraduates. I therefore urge the government to establish national scholarships. These scholarships would be awarded on a competitive basis and the recipient would be allowed to attend any accredited university in Canada. Such a system of scholarships would remove any fears a provincial government might have that the federal government was interfering in the field of education.
There is another suggestion, however, and this has to do with the university loan fund for students. I understand that the University of British Columbia holds promissory notes from students for some $200,000. I am also advised that these notes are 99.9 per cen' good, because while it may take the student a long time to repay them they are ultimately repaid. I have no knowledge as to the amount of the funds available at other universities, but I think the integrity of the Canadian university student is the same. That being so, in order to keep the loan funds circulating I would suggest that the federal treasury discount these notes. Thus the government might even make a small profit, and the universities would have more money to loan without having to wait a long time for the money to be repaid. If the government does not consider this suggestion feasible, then I would suggest that the Canada Council, with its huge endowment and its declared purpose of encouraging Canadian art and culture, should investigate this problem facing the universities.
I now wish to speak about old age pensioners, of whom I have a very large number in my constituency. Time and time again I receive letters from these pensioners asking why they cannot receive the pension if they go outside the country. I know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) has received many representations on this subject, and I assure him that I appreciate the administrative problems which make the payment of pensions outside of Canada difficult. Nonetheless, while the administrative problems present difficulties, I believe they can be overcome. One of the more minor problems is that of identification, and I would therefore offer to the government
The Budget-Mr. Jung this suggestion. Why not issue a small identification card to the pensioner when he first qualifies for his pension? This card might be similar to the small wallet-sized card issued on request by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and which has a picture of the applicant sealed between plastic covers. Such a card would be very satisfactory identification, because not only does the card bear his picture but it also bears his signature. I do not think that any bank would hesitate to accept or recognize such identification. If the government is concerned with the possibility of fraud or that the pension cheque might fall into the wrong hands, such an identification card might be one solution.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to my last subject, and that is the matter of housing. My constituency, Mr. Speaker, is a most unique riding. In recent years great changes have occurred, particularly in the residential area known as the west end. Old houses are being torn down daily and apartment blocks are springing up like mushrooms. One of the most urgent problems brought about by this rapid change is the need for space for stores. The west end has its own shopping district, but thee is a danger of the small stores disappearing because as more and more land is taken over for apartments it becomes correspondingly difficult to find space for stores. At present Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not lend money on apartments it there are stores in those apartments. This might be a good time for the government to consider amending the National Housing Act to permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to lend money to build apartments which would have stores on the ground floor.
Hon. members will see that this plan might have some possibilities. Apartment blocks could be built to replace the present old business blocks and at the same time retain the small stores which are such an attraction and convenience to the apartment dwellers. I do not visualize huge supermarkets being built into these apartments but rather shops selling ladies' and men's wear, dry cleaners, drug stores, beauty parlours, small restaurants and other shops offering necessary services on a small scale. I am also convinced that this type of apartment can be designed so as to be functional and yet satisfy the aesthetic senses of those living in the apartment. For example, one might consider an arcade type of apartment. Again, these stores could form the perimeter of a court yard, or the stores could be built facing the street, with the apartment block set back a little and joined to the stores.

The Budget-Mr. Jung
I can get quite enthusiastic over the design possibilities, but what is more important is that I am convinced this type of apartment would fill a very useful and urgent need, particularly in areas like Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. I know that the west end business association of my riding would be very grateful to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) if this scheme could be introduced. The Minister of Public Works has established an outstanding reputation for the highly competent way in which he has administered his department, and I believe that one reason for the minister's popularity is his readiness to listen to suggestions and his approachability. I therefore offer this suggestion to him in the hope that his department will explore the possibilities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks today have ranged over a wide field. In ranging from the need of further financial assistance to university students to the need for awakening every Canadian to the economic war which has been declared by the communists on us, I have done so with one object in mind, and that is the welfare of our country. Our country is recovering from a recession. Notwithstanding this recovery, serious doubts about our future welfare come to my mind when I see various groups acting only in their own interests and without regard for the consequences which some of their acts will have upon other innocent parties. Yet when some of these groups get into trouble because of their actions, they cry and run to the government for help.
Government has its obligations but so does every group within the state, be it business or labour. There appears to be no diminishing of this pattern of activity. Everywhere you turn you hear the question "Why does the government not do something about it?" or "Let the government do it". Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that what many call government assistance or intervention may turn out in the end to be discipline by the state. Phrased in that way, many of us might take a second look at our habit of running to the government for a cure when, as is so often the case, the solution lies within the means of the parties involved.
No one likes discipline and to avoid unnecessary discipline we must first learn how to discipline ourselves. This does not necessarily mean sacrifice but it does mean the practice of moderation in our demands and a more mature acceptance of our responsibilities to others. The Minister of Finance in his budget has given us our terms of reference. I hope that with this new awareness of our responsibilities Canadians everywhere will indeed face the future with confidence in our ability, courage in our actions and faith in our country.

Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transport):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:-
1.	For purposes of economy in construction, operation and maintenance, the lock filling and emptying systems at St. Lambert, Cote Ste. Catherine and Beauharnois were standardized. The design, confirmed by model studies, provides for the raising or lowering of water level in a lock of the maximum lift of 45 feet (Beauharnois) in 8 minutes.
